newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Serbian students keep up 24-hour vigil.
newsitem.headline: Serbian students keep up 24-hour vigil.

text.p: Serbian students kept up a round-the-clock vigil against election fraud on Saturday but ruling Socialists showed no sign they were ready to back down despite nearly 70 days of opposition demonstrations.

Students from the Belgrade medical faculty braved bitter cold to gather in front of a police cordon in a stand-off that began last Sunday when police blocked attempts to hold a march through the city centre.
University students and many of their professors have organised a 24-hour vigil in a bid to wait out the police cordon, rotating groups of students in shifts.

President Slobodan Milosevic has relied on his vast police force and his state television station to try to stifle a wave of street demonstrations demanding authorities recognise opposition victories in November municipal elections.
The opposition Zajedno (Together) coalition, supported by students, planned to stage the 69th consecutive day of demonstrations on Saturday.
Zajedno has accused the Socialist authorities of refusing to endorse opposition victories in 14 of Serbia's biggest cities.
Milosevic's Socialists discussed the unprecedented threat to five decades of unbroken communist and socialist rule at a session of the party's central committee on Friday.

Belgrade independent media reported party officials were ready to enlist the help of hardline nationalists from the Serbian Radical Party to shore up their position and help them portray the opposition as traitors.
The independent daily "Nasa Borba", citing unnamed sources, said the party was planning a government reshuffle and a renewed media assault on the Zajedno opposition.

The Zajedno protests that have swept Belgrade and cities across the country represented an "attack on the state by the same people who broke the old Yugoslavia," the paper quoted Milosevic as saying at the session.
The protests -- marked by an irreverent, carnival atmosphere -- have won strong Western support and sparked divisions within the Socialist ranks.

Milosevic has remained aloof and out of public view during the crisis while his deputies and state media have sent out mixed signals, shifting from promises of concessions to stern warnings and communist-style rhetoric.
The United States has led Western pressure against Milosevic to accept the opposition victories but the former communist party chief has refused to budge.
Party leaders met amid signs the police were taking an increasingly tough line against demonstrators.
Riot police on Thursday clubbed protesters seated on a highway into the central town of Kragujevac, beating one member of parliament unconscious.

Independent radio stations B-92 and Index, citing accounts by witnesses, reported beatings in several Belgrade districts as police ambushed small groups of people making their way to the student vigil on Friday.
Three other opposition deputies were beaten and arrested in the towns of Cacak, Kraljevo and Krusevac, Zajedno leaders said.
The creeping violence has failed to discourage opposition supporters. The student vigil on Friday night turned into a big open-air disco with thousands of people dancing past midnight.
